clue.text: Hairline fractures finally seen in window that's not new — tip!

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word before it, so take the last letter of 'fractures'
new is abbreviated N, so 'not new' strips that letter out of 'window'

parts.note: a tip is a peak, the pointed top of something

explanation.surface: Someone spots hairline cracks in an old window and passes on a handy tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairline fractures' reads as one phrase about cracked glass, but 'Hairline' stands alone as the definition. The dash and exclamation make 'tip' look like advice; it is a pointed top.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a V-shaped point of hair at the middle of the forehead is one particular hairline.

clue.text: Aha! Somewhere to get a drink!

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of surprise or discovery
a shaft sunk into the ground to draw water

explanation.surface: Someone thirsty cries out on spotting a place to get a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does two jobs: WELL is both an exclamation and a source of water. The surface makes it one delighted moment of discovery.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: 'Well!' as an interjection of surprise, and a well as a water source.

clue.text: Twice act the fool

indicators.note: twice means two times, so the next piece is written out twice

parts.note: the same two letters a second time

explanation.surface: An instruction to play the clown not once but twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act the fool' reads as one idiom, but it splits: 'act' is the wordplay and 'fool' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense: the extinct flightless bird lends its name to a stupid or behind-the-times person.

clue.text: Pa, can we read novel — a big one?

indicators.note: as an adjective novel means new, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A child asks their father whether they can tackle a novel together – a really big one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' works twice: as an adjective meaning new it rearranges the letters, and as a noun it starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Tolstoy's book runs to well over a thousand pages, the byword for a very long novel.

clue.text: Forecaster making net gains in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: net gains are what a business keeps after costs; spoken, it matches a word for a seer

explanation.surface: A pundit whose predictions pay off when he speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making' is the link. 'Net' is not fishing gear but the sense left after deductions.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who foretells what is coming.

clue.text: Warned: treadle malfunctioning

indicators.note: a malfunctioning machine has its parts out of order, and so do these letters

explanation.surface: A notice that the foot pedal on a sewing machine has broken.
explanation.walkthrough: A treadle is a foot-operated pedal driving a machine such as an old sewing machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: put on guard about a danger.

clue.text: He's in the OT in biblical tower, scratching head

indicators.note: to scratch is to strike out, so the head, the first letter, goes

parts.note: the Tower of Babel in Genesis
the first letter of that tower's name, struck out

explanation.surface: A figure from the Old Testament stands puzzled in the Tower of Babel.
explanation.walkthrough: OT is the Old Testament. 'Scratching head' looks like puzzlement, which suits Babel's confusion of tongues.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Adam and Eve's second son, killed by Cain, is one of the Old Testament's figures.

clue.text: Small bird illegally traded? I bet

indicators.note: done illegally means not by the rules, so the letters are not in their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a small bird has been sold on the black market.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'I bet' read as a speaker's sceptical aside, but all those letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a small tawny reed-bed bird whose male has black 'moustache' markings.

clue.text: Sadly hit by snarl where dead ends abound

definitions.note: the definition describes a kind of place; the answer is plural

indicators.note: sadly can mean in a sorry state, badly done, so the letters are in a mess

explanation.surface: Someone snarled at in a place where every road seems to lead nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snarl' also means a tangle, which fits a maze nicely, but here it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: By description: mazes are built of branching paths, most of them closed off.

clue.text: Short trousers and red heels on, dancing

indicators.note: dancers move about and swap places, and the letters do the same

explanation.surface: A dancer kitted out in shorts and red heels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' reads as joining two items of clothing; it only links definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: By description: the leather shorts of Bavarian and Austrian folk dress.

clue.text: Clothing to boast about

indicators.note: to turn about is to turn round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to boast is to brag, and those four letters are set down from the back

explanation.surface: An outfit worth showing off about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' after 'boast'; it turns the boast round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually for distinctive dress: clerical garb.

clue.text: It's almost always off the charts

definitions.text: It's almost always off the charts

parts.note: not quite always: there was one exception
the surface pushes 'extraordinary'; taken literally it means absent from the pop charts

explanation.surface: Something so extreme it is literally off the scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the charts' usually means extraordinary; read literally it means absent from the pop charts, where this act appeared only once.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for an artist known for a single hit record, and so almost never in the charts.

clue.text: Clear at the outset, Everyman's on rugby pitch, unwell and too old

indicators.note: the outset is the start, so this piece comes first
in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next

parts.note: the goalposts on a rugby pitch are H-shaped

explanation.surface: The setter, out on the rugby field, admits feeling poorly and past it.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is also the setter's name, so the clue sounds like a self-portrait; here it just gives HE. The 's is 'is', letting HE sit on top of H in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: past one's prime, like someone who has climbed to the top and is on the way down.

clue.text: Bob Marley song I Shot the Sheriff's intro, live, remastered

indicators.note: a remastered track is reworked, so the letters are rearranged
the intro of a piece is its opening, so take the first letter

explanation.surface: A live, remastered recording of the opening to Marley's I Shot the Sheriff.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title 'I Shot the Sheriff' must be broken apart: 'I Shot' is taken whole, but only the S of 'Sheriff'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a 1978 single by Bob Marley and the Wailers.

clue.text: In line? I nearly ran, being obstinate

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

parts.note: a flex is British for an electric cable or cord
ran = BLED, as colours do in the wash, less its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone in a queue confesses they almost ran off, being too stubborn to wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran' is not running but colours running in the wash: BLED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: unwilling to bend or change one's mind.

clue.text: Constituents of saliva in play area?

parts.note: saliva = spit; its first letter is one constituent
listing the parts joins them with 'and'
the rest of spit is the other constituent

explanation.surface: A question about what is in the spit found in a children's play area.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: SPIT is made of the parts S and PIT, and the phrase describing that, 'S and PIT', spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sand-filled hollow where children dig and play.

clue.text: André's denounced, to some extent, somewhere on the Elbe …

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of the phrase is used

explanation.surface: André has been denounced somewhere along a German river.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into the next clue, but each clue is solved on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital of Saxony, in eastern Germany, straddles the River Elbe.

clue.text: … French president losing energy in part of Benelux

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so the letter goes

explanation.surface: A former French president runs out of energy in the Low Countries.
explanation.walkthrough: Benelux is Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose sense: the name of the Netherlands' western provinces is widely used for the whole country, one of the three Benelux states.

clue.text: Diminish empty, desolate expanse

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: a tract is an expanse of land

explanation.surface: A bleak, empty wasteland that shrinks away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' and 'desolate' look like two synonyms side by side; the first empties the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually followed by 'from': to lessen the worth of something.

clue.text: He ignores issues over case of suet that's fattening

parts.note: O = over, as in cricket scoring

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so take the outer letters

explanation.surface: Someone ignoring warnings about a suet pudding's calories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issues over' reads as one phrase; 'over' is O. Suet is hard animal fat used in British puddings.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the bird is said to bury its head in the sand, so a person who refuses to face problems is called one.

clue.text: Characters from Tinseltown go along to see player's worst fear

indicators.note: characters are letters, so take some of the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Hollywood actors go along to watch a footballer's nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters from Tinseltown' looks like film stars and makes 'Tinseltown' seem the only source; the letters run on through 'go along'.
explanation.definitionFit: By description: putting the ball into your own net is the mistake every footballer dreads.

clue.text: What you expect with cricket: below lifeless

parts.note: a cricket, the insect, has six legs, each with a foot

explanation.surface: A complaint that watching cricket is deathly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cricket' is the insect, not the game, and the number is a count of legs rather than a hit to the boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: buried in a grave, so dead.

clue.text: Proudly impenitent artiste française, primarily!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A tribute to a French singer who was proud to regret nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: Édith Piaf sang 'Non, je ne regrette rien', a proud refusal to repent.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the French chanteuse's signature song declares she regrets nothing.

clue.text: River goddess

definitions.meaning: the Thames takes a different name as it flows through Oxford
the Egyptian mother goddess, wife of Osiris

explanation.walkthrough: The Thames is called the Isis in Oxford, a favourite crossword river.
explanation.definitionFit: Two proper names that happen to coincide: an Oxford stretch of the Thames and an Egyptian deity.

clue.text: Brother repulsed by small globes

indicators.note: repulsed means driven back, so the word is turned round

parts.note: bro = brother, pushed back so it reads from the end

explanation.surface: A brother is disgusted by some little balls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repulsed' looks like disgust; it means driven back, which reverses BRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spheres, like the jewelled ball a monarch holds.

clue.text: Greatest parts of capitals etc with carbon reduction

indicators.note: reducing something makes it smaller, here by one letter

parts.note: capitals and the like are major cities
C = carbon, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: A study of carbon cuts in the biggest parts of capital cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an environmental report; 'with carbon reduction' means take C out of MAJOR CITIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the larger shares of a whole, as in a vote.

clue.text: 50 / 50 = odd? No
Even so, sentences that depict fruit etc

definitions.note: elliptical: read as '[pictures] that depict fruit etc'

explanation.surface: A remark about sentences that describe bowls of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentences' are prison terms, not grammar. The painting's plural keeps the F.
explanation.definitionFit: By description: paintings of arranged objects such as fruit, flowers and jugs.
